title: Independence of P versus NP from ZFC
why: This asks whether the usual foundations of mathematics can decide a central finite computational question. Fixing the theory separates limitations of particular methods from limits of the full axiom system.
status_note: Fortnow’s pointer and Aaronson’s survey were checked on 14 September 2026. They motivate the independence question and distinguish weak theories from strong set theories. A bounded later-work search did not verify a full resolution of this ZFC target; unverified claims of P versus NP resolutions are not treated as theorems. The ZFC specialization and explicit arithmetization are editorial choices responding to public feedback, not a newly proved independence result.

sentences: P versus NP asks whether efficiently verifiable decisions can always be made efficiently.
This card asks specifically whether ZFC proves neither the usual arithmetic statement P = NP nor its negation.
It defines that statement through polynomial-time deterministic satisfiability and allows all finite ZFC proofs.
Results for restricted theories and oracle machines do not establish the asserted independence from full ZFC.
The question has a definite yes/no target once the axioms are fixed, and a positive answer would also imply their consistency.

definitions:
SAT is the language of satisfiable finite Boolean formulas built from variables, NOT, binary AND and binary OR. Fix the following binary prefix encoding: a variable with positive index i is 00 followed by 1^l 0 and the l-bit binary representation of i, where l is the bit length of i; NOT is 01 followed by one encoded formula; AND is 10 followed by two encoded formulas; OR is 11 followed by two encoded formulas. A valid string must encode exactly one complete formula. Invalid strings are outside SAT. Truth assignments map the finitely many variables occurring in a formula to Boolean values, with the usual truth tables for the three connectives.

The sentence \(\sigma\) is the usual finite-computation arithmetization of: there exist a deterministic Turing machine M and positive integers c,k such that, for every binary string x, M halts within \(c(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and outputs 1 exactly when x is in SAT, and 0 otherwise. Machines have a finite transition table, a two-way infinite tape, a finite tape alphabet containing the binary input symbols and blank, a start state, and accepting and rejecting halting states; each transition reads and writes one symbol, changes state, and moves the head by at most one cell. The input is written consecutively starting at the initial head position, with blank elsewhere. There is no oracle, advice or randomness. Finite strings, transition tables and computation histories are encoded by natural numbers. Standard effective encodings of these finite objects give ZFC-provably equivalent sentences, so the target is invariant under their choice. SAT is NP-complete, making this the conventional P = NP sentence.

ZFC means classical first-order set theory in the language of membership and equality, with extensionality, empty set, pairing, union, power set, infinity, foundation, choice, and the separation and replacement schemas for all first-order formulas with parameters. Arithmetic is interpreted on its natural numbers, with finite strings and machine computations encoded there. The notation \(\mathrm{ZFC}\vdash\tau\) means that there is a finite derivation of \(\tau\) using these axioms in a sound and complete classical first-order proof calculus with equality; equivalent standard calculi give the same derivable sentences. There is no proof-length bound, extra soundness axiom, oracle, or restriction to a weak fragment of arithmetic. Both unprovability assertions range over all finite derivations in the ordinary metatheory.

The question asks for actual syntactic independence, without building a consistency hypothesis into the proposition. A positive answer entails that ZFC is consistent; inconsistency would make both sentences derivable and hence make this independence claim false. If an argument assumes Con(ZFC) or stronger principles, those assumptions must remain explicit. Choosing ZFC makes the source's general independence discussion into one definite yes/no question; it does not claim that independence from every possible axiom system is equivalent.

context_blocks.text: Fortnow’s further-reading section points to Aaronson’s survey on formal independence. The choice of an axiom system is essential: changing the theory changes the proposition whose provability is being asked about. This card now selects ZFC explicitly in response to the public note.

Aaronson surveys unprovability results for weak theories, including conditional bounded-arithmetic results. These delimit particular formal methods; they do not establish independence from full ZFC. Likewise, opposite relativizations concern oracle computations and do not by themselves yield the two ZFC unprovability assertions.

Syntactic independence concerns what the named axioms can prove, while P versus NP concerns the existence of an algorithm in the standard finite computational model. These are different claims, even though the arithmetic sentence about the algorithm is the subject of the independence question.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the two stated unprovability assertions, or their logical negation: \(\mathrm{ZFC}\vdash\sigma\) or \(\mathrm{ZFC}\vdash\neg\sigma\). Derivability must concern the specified SAT sentence and full ZFC. A proof only about a weaker theory, bounded-length proofs, an oracle version, or an unrelated strengthened statement does not settle this target. An independence theorem conditional on consistency settles only that explicitly conditional version unless its assumption is also established.

community_reviews.original_text: This is not a yes/no question. It depends on the proof system. I think for some very limited proof systems the answer is known to be that P vs NP is independent. Perhaps one would have to specify whether it is independent of say ZFC - Zernel-Frankl theroy with axion of choice.
community_reviews.response: Specified full ZFC, the arithmetic SAT sentence, finite formal derivability and the consistency convention. With the theory fixed this is a yes/no question. Results for weak theories are distinguished from independence of full ZFC.
